extracted.intended_audience: engineers, process-safety professionals, and risk assessors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting and documenting engineering risk assessments and cost–benefit analyses for safety-related design decisions, including how to choose values, estimate units, set risk-tolerance criteria, and prepare analyses that may become public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cost–benefit analyses for safety decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: At issue for engineers is whether risk assessments and cost-benefit analyses are appropriate when considering safety. The answer must be yes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources are finite and must be allocated; if not by rational analysis they will be allocated based on visceral emotional responses. Use cost–benefit analysis as a tool to allocate resources rationally when considering safety measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate valuation of human life (Value of a Statistical Life, VSL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much has been made of Ford’s (actually the NHTSA’s) value of life of 'only $200,000'. Nowadays, no one would use discounted future earnings as a basis for placing an economic value on a statistical human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modern, accepted VSL estimates (examples given: EPA $9.1M, FDA $7.9M, DOT $6.0M) rather than outdated low figures. Choice of VSL materially changes results; document and justify the VSL used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately estimate number of affected incidents/units
rubrics_metrics.description: Another difficulty in estimating benefits is in estimating the number of units. Ford estimated the number of deaths at 180 per year; other sources estimated 500 or 2,000; actual NHTSA data for 1971–77 showed 38 rear-end Pinto collisions with fire, 27 deaths and 24 non-fatal burn injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base unit counts on best available empirical data, not sensational or extrapolated figures. Be explicit about the period, denominator (e.g., vehicles produced), and sources. Where uncertainty is large, show ranges and sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define scope and hazard scenario clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The memo considered the entire fleet of cars and light trucks and rollovers; it never once mentioned the Ford Pinto and was about rollovers, not rear-end collisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit which vehicles, crash modes, and failure scenarios are covered. Misalignment between analysis scope and the criticized event (e.g., rollover vs rear-end collision) invites misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat costs in the correct distributive context (societal vs per-model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The costs to society were $11 per vehicle because the requirement would apply to the entire market — not just Pintos or Fords — and manufacturing costs are passed along to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether cost estimates are per-unit, per-model, or market-wide (societal). When a regulatory fix applies market-wide, multiply per-unit costs by the full affected production base; document that reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document assumptions and prepare for public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such thing as an 'internal' document. Your analyses and your risk tolerance criteria will become public. Perform your assessments and analyses as though the public is looking over your shoulder. They are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write analyses with clear assumptions, methods, and provenance. Anticipate external scrutiny and potential media attention; avoid informal language or hidden caveats that could be misrepresented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of analysis relative to design decisions matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The memo was written more than three years after the Pinto went into production, long after the Pinto’s design was complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct cost–benefit and risk assessments at stages where they can inform design choices. Post-hoc analyses that occur after production or final design are less defensible as decision documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use current, robust economic and methodological practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the 1970s, economists have studied valuation extensively and have developed more accepted methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt contemporary valuation methods (VSL and injury monetization) and avoid outdated bases like discounted future earnings without justification. Cite sources and contemporary agency practice where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and communicate uncertainty — costs easier to estimate than benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: It is always easier to estimate the cost of a safety measure than the benefit of a safety measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sensitivity analyses, ranges, and scenario testing to show how results change with different assumptions (VSL, incident counts, cost per unit). Explicitly call out which inputs are most uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and document risk tolerance criteria explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: The fault was not in the analysis, but in the risk tolerance criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define acceptable risk thresholds and decision rules up front. Explain how societal, legal, ethical, and stakeholder values informed chosen risk-tolerance criteria and how they affect the final recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate context to avoid media/public misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The media, advocates, and politicians still refer to the Pinto Memo as the basis for condemning Ford; the memo has been mischaracterized (e.g., framed as a decision to 'let ’em burn').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear summaries, state limitations, and avoid ambiguous phrasing that can be sensationalized. Anticipate common misreads (wrong scope, wrong unit counts) and address them proactively in communication materials.
